text: A partial differential equation can produce a beautiful animation.
But what makes that picture useful for research?
We need to see the model, check the calculation, and keep the evidence.
This is PhaseAtlas: a visual workbench that connects those steps.
Start with an equation and the question you want to investigate.
In the Studio, researchers can edit the model, initial data, and boundary conditions.
Supported models include coupled evolution equations and fourth-order problems.
The numerical method and its limits stay visible, so users can choose an appropriate experiment.

The result is more than an animation.
Researchers can export the model, parameters, trajectories, and numerical checks, alongside figures and video.
Selected problems can be compared with an independent Python implementation.
Computation runs on the user's device.
That makes the workflow accessible for exploring a model, checking an idea, and sharing a
reproducible calculation.
Here is the workflow in the live Studio.
Start from a heat-transfer model, then edit the equation and its parameters.
Type the spatial derivatives directly into the equation box.
I will use diffusion on a one-dimensional rod, with heat exchange at both ends.
Each boundary has its own coefficients, so we can change the environment without rewriting the
solver. The left and right ends can also use different boundary data.
Now run the experiment. Play the saved solution, pause it, or scrub through time to
inspect a particular frame. Then choose Check resolution.
The platform reruns the model with a smaller time step and a finer grid, and
reports the differences. This comparison is something we can actually check.
Finally, export the experiment as JSON.
It includes the configuration, the saved fields, and the numerical checks, so another researcher can
inspect and reproduce the calculation.
The longer-term goal is a research platform that helps people ask better mathematical questions and
inspect the evidence together. I am Niu Te from Imperial College London.
This is PhaseAtlas.
